title: John Belushi
wiki_lead:
John Adam Belushi ( bə-LOO-shee; January 24, 1949 – March 5, 1982) was an American comedian, actor, and musician. He was one of seven Saturday Night Live cast members of the first season. Belushi had a working partnership with Dan Aykroyd; they had first met while at Chicago's the Second City comedy club, remaining together as cast members on Saturday Night Live.
Born in Chicago to Albanian-American parents, Belushi started his own comedy troupe with Tino Insana and Steve Beshekas, called "The West Compass Trio". Bernard Sahlins recruited him for The Second City comedy club. Once there he met Aykroyd, Brian Doyle-Murray, and Harold Ramis. In 1975, Chevy Chase and Michael O'Donoghue recommended Belushi to Saturday Night Live creator and showrunner Lorne Michaels, who accepted him as a new cast member of the show after an audition. Belushi developed a series of characters on the show that reached great success, including Henry Kissinger and Ludwig van Beethoven.
Belushi appeared in several films such as National Lampoon's Animal House, 1941, The Blues Brothers, and Neighbors. He also pursued interests in music; with Aykroyd, Lou Marini, Tom Malone, Steve Cropper, Donald "Duck" Dunn, and Paul Shaffer, he founded The Blues Brothers, which led to the film of the same name.
Belushi was dismissed from Saturday Night Live several times and rehired more than once. He died on March 5, 1982, at the age of 33. Cathy Smith confessed to dosing him with a lethal mixture of heroin and cocaine at the Chateau Marmont. Smith was charged with involuntary manslaughter, and was convicted and sentenced to 15 months in prison. Belushi was honored with a posthumous award of the star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2004. He was the older brother of Jim Belushi.

Early life and education

John Adam Belushi was born to Agnes Demetri (née  Samaras) Belushi and Adam Anastos Belushi in Humboldt Park, Chicago. Agnes was a pharmacy worker, who was born in Ohio to Albanian immigrants from Korçë, Albania. Adam Anastos Belushi was an Albanian immigrant from Qytezë, Albania, and was the owner of the Fair Oaks restaurant on North Avenue in Chicago.
Belushi was raised in Wheaton along with his three siblings—younger brothers Billy and Jim and sister Marian. He was Eastern Orthodox Christian, attending the Albanian Orthodox Church. He was educated at Wheaton Central High School, where he met his future wife, Judith Jacklin.
In 1965, Belushi formed a band, the Ravens, together with four fellow high-school students (Dick Blasucci, Michael Blasucci, Tony Pavilonis, and Phil Special). They recorded one single, "Listen to Me Now/Jolly Green Giant". Belushi played drums and sang vocals. The record was not successful, and the band broke up when he enrolled at the College of DuPage. During the summer of 1967, after graduating from high school, he was hired to perform in several plays at the Shawnee Summer Theatre of Greene County in Bloomfield, IN. grok_lead: John Adam Belushi (January 24, 1949 â March 5, 1982) was an American comedian, actor, and musician of Albanian descent, best known for his high-energy performances as a cast member on the sketch comedy series Saturday Night Live and as the lead singer Jake Blues in the musical comedy duo the Blues Brothers. Born in Chicago, Illinois, to Albanian immigrant Adam Belushi, a restaurant owner, and Agnes Samaras Belushi, of Albanian heritage, Belushi was the eldest of four children and displayed an early talent for humor and athletics, serving as captain of his high school football team. After briefly attending the University of WisconsinâWhitewater, he transferred to the College of DuPage, where he dropped out to pursue comedy full-time, starting with an improvisational troupe called the West Compass Players. Belushi's professional career began in 1971 when he joined the Mainstage cast of The Second City improv theater in Chicago, where his dynamic stage presence quickly gained attention. In 1973, he moved to New York as a writer and performer for the National Lampoon Radio Hour, collaborating with future Saturday Night Live colleagues like Dan Aykroyd, Gilda Radner, and Bill Murray. This experience led to his casting as one of the original repertory players on Saturday Night Live when it premiered in 1975, where he remained until 1979, creating memorable characters such as the Samurai Futaba and the bee from the "Killer Bees" sketches. During his SNL tenure, Belushi expanded into film with his breakout role as John "Bluto" Blutarsky in the 1978 comedy National Lampoon's Animal House, which became a cultural phenomenon and grossed over $141 million at the box office. He and Aykroyd developed the Blues Brothers act on SNL in 1978, blending soul and blues music with comedy, which evolved into the 1980 feature film The Blues Brothers, directed by John Landis and featuring a soundtrack that revitalized interest in classic R&B artists. Belushi's film career continued with roles in 1941 (1979), The Blues Brothers, Continental Divide (1981), and Neighbors (1981), showcasing his range from slapstick to dramatic elements. Belushi's personal life was marked by his 1976 marriage to Judy Jacklin, whom he met in high school, and his growing struggles with substance abuse amid the pressures of fame. On March 5, 1982, at age 33, he died in a bungalow at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Hollywood from acute cocaine and heroin intoxication, an event that shocked the entertainment world and highlighted the era's drug culture in comedy. His death prompted widespread tributes, and his brother Jim Belushi later carried on aspects of his legacy in film and music, including leading the Blues Brothers 2000 band.
